CODE OF PRACTICE FOR STEEL CYLINDERS FOR COMPRESSED GASES
PART 7 AMMONIA GAS ( First Revision) . Scope - Covers filling, inspection, testing, maintenance and use of portable steel cylinders for the torage and transportation of liquefied ammonia gas in cylinders, of nominal capacity UP to and lcluding 130 litres water capacity. 3.2 Ignition Range in Air - 15 to 30 percent by volume. This means that within this range of concentration. the gas is capable of forming mixtures with air in which at an initial temperature of 20�C and an at initial pressure of 1 atmosphere, there is propagation of ignition, started by an ignition source. 3.3 Maximum Permissible Toxicity - 100 ppm by volume. (This is the maximum concentration in air to which nearly all workers may be exposed day after day without adverse effects. ) Inhalation of air containing more than 5 000 ppm of ammonia may cause death. Permanent eye injury may result from exposure to 700 ppm concentrations for longer than 30 minutes. 3.4 Chemical Reaction with Metals - When dry, ammonia .does not react with-most of the metals. When mixed with even very little water, it vigorously attacks copper, zinc, silver and many alloys, especially those containing copper. Hence absolutely no brass or bronze valve fittings are to be used for ammonia cylinders. Fittings should be made of iron or steel since ammonia will not attack these materials. 4. Approved Specifications and General Guidance for Manufacture

4.1 The cylinders used for the storage and transportation of ammonia gas shall conform to one of the specifications approved by statutory authority. A list of approved specifications for filling in this country is available with the Chief Controller ~of Explosives, Nagpur. 4.2 Cylinders manufactured in accordance with approved specifications shall be provided with an It shall be borne in mind that corrosion additional wall thickness to allow for corrosion during service. is not related to the thickness of the container so that any additional thickness allowed for corrosion should be constant rather than a given proportion of thickness. 4.3 Further, additional wall thickness shall also be considered necessary in order that the cylinder can safely withstand stresses due to horizontal acceleration and retardation in normal road transportation. The cylinder shall be so designed that the maximum permissible equivalent stress will not be exceeded when the stresses in the cylinder due to vertical accelerations are super imposed upon the stress due to internal pressure. The vertical acceleration considered should be those occurring in normal road transport. The provisions to be made in these and other respects as well was manufacturing tolerances to be applied will generally be decided between the user and the manufacturer. If a pronounced departure from normal practice is proposed or if other unusual features arise, the statutory authority shall be consulted. 5. 9.2.1 The manufacturer IO. Storage 10.1 Cylinders shall be stored in a dry ventilated place away from excessive heat or danger of fire, and protected from accumulation of snow and ice. It is preferable that cylinder storage room be fire-~proof. The storage room shall not be used for any purpose other than the storage of cylinders. 10.2 Ventilation shall be provided through the structure in such a manner that full advantage of natural ventilation may be obtained. If natural ventilation is not sufficient, then storage area shall be equipped with suitable type at mechanical ventilation. 10.3 Pocketing of ammonia gas under floor roofs and similar structures shall be avoided. other page of the label shall contain of the content and details of filler. the details of cylinder, content of the cylinders,

10.4 Locations used for storage of cylinders shall be cut off from other occupancies and the building protected with automatic sprinklers, vapour-tight electrical equipments, good natural ventilation, good floor drainage and adequate explosion venting. 10.5 Cylinders shall never be stored near gangways or elevators or near ventilating systems.

10.6 Dangers can be reduced by storing cylinders

so that the oldest stock can be used first.

10.7 Keeping the full and empty cylinders separately and storing in an orderly way will reduce the necessary handling and confusion and permit frequent inspection for signs of leaks or other dangers. Valve protection hoods shall always be kept in place except when cylinders are actually being emptied. 10.8 Cylinders 10.9 Cylinders shall be stored in an upright shall not be stored outdoor. position.

11.3 Hoisting of cylinders is not recommended. However, if hoisting connot be avoided, a lifting clamp cradle or carrier shall always be used. Ammonia cylinders shall never be hoisted with lifting magnet, rope or chain sling. A cylinder shall never be lifted by the hood as it is not strong enough to support the weight. 11.4 The cylinders shall not be used as rollers to move other equipment. equipped trucks and dollies may be used for moving the

14. Discharge Two general types of valves 14.1 The tube type cylinder is normally used in the horizontal position. Depending on which type is involved, either the valve outlet or the valve stem is kept are supplied. The position of this valve outlet or stem at an angle with the longitudinal axis of the cylinder. When the valve ~determines whether liquid or gaseous ammonia will be discharged from the cylinder. outlet or stem is on top, the dip pipe on the inside of the cylinder is under the liquid, and, therefore, liquid anhydrous ammonia will be discharged. To discharge gaseous ammonia, the cylinder is turned For this, instructions of the concerned ammonia so that the valve outlet or stem points downward. manufacturer shall be followed. 14.2 The bottle type or vertical type will discharge ammonia as a gas when placed in an upright or Due to liquid ammonia expansion, a bottle type cylinder may, under certain vertical position. elevated temperature conditions, discharge a small amount of liquid when the valve is opened. It is, therefore, recommended that bottle type cylinders be allowed to reach room temperature before To discharge liquid anhydrous ammonia, this type of cylinder shall be placed in the valve is opened. a horizontal position with the valve outlet pointed up. 14.3 The rate at which gaseous ammonia may be discharged from either type cylinders depends the temperature of the surrounding atmosphere and the surface area of the liquid ammonia. 14.4 When the cylinder is empty, it should cylinder protective cap replaced. be disconnected and the valve plug inserted and upon

17. Ammonia 17.1 Ammonia

Leaks and Spills leaks shall always be taken care of immediately or they will become worse.

17.2 Leaks of ammonia shall be searched ~for, pFeferably with hydrochloric acid solution or with either chlorine gas or sulphur dioxide gas, using a small cylinder of the compressed gas. A white cloud is Because of the fire risk, sulphur candies should not be used. produced in the presence of ammonia. 17.3 If leaks or spills occur, only protected personnel should remain in the area. In case where leaks cannot be valved off, large volumes of water shall be sprayed directly on the leak and the contact Leaking cylinders shall be removed to the maintai'ned until the contents have been discharged. outdoors or to an isolated well-ventilated area and the contents transferred to other suitable containers. All spills shall be flushed away promptly with water. 17.4 Corrective 17.5 17.6 measures shall be undertaken only by trained men wearing proper safety equipments.

If the leak is large, all persons in the affected area shall be warned. If ammonia is leaking as liquid, the cylinder shall be turned so that the leaking side is on the top.

17.7 Leaks around valve stem, valve discharge the packing gland or replacing gaskets. 17.8 A leaking container

outlet shall be stopped by closing the valve or tightening

EXPLANATORY

NOTE

For safe handling of cylinders containing liquid ammonia, one should be thoroughly conversant There are several precautions and safe practices with the properties and characteristics of ammonia. which are to be observed on account of the nature of ammonia and also because of the pressure to which cylinders are subjected. Manufacturers, fillers, and users of the gas cylinders covered by this code should be familiar with the precautions laid down in this code in order to ensure safe and efficient operating conditions. For general information on different gases conveyed in cylinders, SP : 9-1973 `Technical data sheet for gases conveyed in cylinders' may also be referred to. This standard was first published in 1979. The committee responsible for preparation of this standard decided to revise the same to bring this standard in line with' the development made in the field of gas cylinder technology at the international level. Other standards Part 1 Part 2 Part 3 Part 4 Part 5 Part ,6 Part 8 Part 9 Part 10 Part 11 in this series, which gases gas gases have also been updated are as under:

Atmospheric Hydrogen

gases

Part 12 Gases for medical

Manufacture, possession and use of any gas when contained in cylinders in a compressed or liquefied form is regulated under the Gas Cylinders Rules 1981, of the Government of India as amended Although the code has been prepared in consultation and agreement with the from time to time. statutory authorities under these rules, should anything in the code conflict with the provisions of Gas Cylinder Rules 1981, the latter shall be adhered to. In using this code, IS : 662-l 980 `Specification for anhydrous lists two grades of anhydrous ammonia shall be borne in mind. ammonia ( first
